title: Research: planner-installed resident reactive programs during model inference
body:
## Motivation

Existing work already covers reactive macros (#6), interrupt scheduling (#14), declarative temporal predicates (#22), bounded local policies (#480), interaction ISA/device lowering (#574/#671), and declarative sensorimotor graphs (#696).

A distinct planner/runtime question remains:

> Can the frontier model install a **temporary resident reactive program** that continuously observes a bounded state, recognizes declared conditions/transitions, and executes pre-authorized local actions while the frontier model is still reasoning — with the model able to interrupt, steer, pause, resume or revoke it asynchronously?

The goal is not another autonomous planner. The goal is to let a slow semantic model leave behind a small, auditable **temporary reflex system** so the computer can keep observing and reacting during model latency.

This directly targets a core Agent Interface bottleneck: the environment may change at millisecond-to-second timescales while frontier-model inference remains much slower.

## Distinction from existing issues

- **#6** contains `WATCH`, servo and background-continuation ideas, but does not isolate the lifecycle of a planner-installed resident recognition+execution program that remains steerable during the next model call.
- **#22** waits for observable predicates and returns evidence; it need not execute task actions.
- **#14** decides which retained events interrupt the planner; it does not define the resident controller itself.
- **#480** allows bounded local policy choice, but the central question here is concurrent execution **during frontier-model inference**, plus asynchronous planner steering of the already-running policy.
- **#696** represents finite static sensorimotor graphs. This issue asks whether an admitted graph/policy can become a live resident process with explicit mailbox/interrupt semantics, trigger memory, temporal patterns and resource ownership across model-thinking intervals.

If the implementation reduces to a one-shot finite graph with no concurrent model interval or steering, keep it under #696 instead.

## Core abstraction

```text
ResidentReactiveProgram {
    program_id
    generation
    intent_id

    sensors[]
    derived_predicates[]
    temporal_patterns[]
    controllers[]
    actuators[]

    rules:
        WHEN predicate       -> one-shot action / controller start
        ON transition        -> one-shot action
        WHILE predicate      -> maintain bounded controller
        UNTIL predicate      -> continue bounded loop
        ON absence/deadline  -> stop / yield
        ON safety event      -> revoke + neutralize

    owned_resources
    allowed_action_subset
    observation_scope
    authority_horizon
    max_duration
    max_transitions
    max_actuator_events
    observation_budget

    interrupt_ports
    safe_points
    retained_events
    release_plan
}
```

The frontier model specifies meaning, predicates, permitted responses and bounds. The runtime may only evaluate declared recognizers and execute already-admitted transitions. It cannot invent a new semantic action.

## Recognition should include transitions, not only states

Persistent programs should support a small bounded family of temporal observables rather than only `predicate == true`:

```text
STATE      target_visible
EDGE       disabled -> enabled
SEQUENCE   spinner_appears -> spinner_disappears -> result_visible
DURATION   condition holds for >= T
ABSENCE    expected condition not observed by deadline
RATE       repeated no-effect >= N within window
COINCIDE   A and B observed in a bounded interval
```

This matters because a persistent true condition must not accidentally fire the same one-shot action every frame.

## Recognition and actuation are separable reusable macros

A useful composition model is:

```text
RecognizerMacro
    TARGET_CENTERED(target, tolerance)

ActuatorMacro
    FIRE_ONCE

Binding
    ON TARGET_CENTERED(target) -> FIRE_ONCE
```

The same recognizer could instead trigger `CLICK`, `DROP`, `YIELD`, or another separately authorized operation. Conversely, the same actuator can be bound to a different recognizer.

This makes the resident program a composition of virtual sensors, temporal predicates and actuators rather than a recorded human workflow.

## Asynchronous planner steering

While the resident program runs, the frontier model may return and modify it through explicit interrupt ports.

Candidate commands:

```text
UPDATE_PARAMETERS
    target / speed / threshold / radius / cadence within frozen bounds

ONE_SHOT
    execute one separately admitted action at next safe point

PAUSE
RESUME
YIELD
REVOKE
```

Each message must name `(program_id, expected_generation)` so a delayed model reply cannot affect a new/restarted controller.

Parameter update must not silently expand the original action/resource/authority envelope. If a change requires new authority, stop/yield and require a new admission.

## Resource arbitration

Concurrent model and resident actions are safe only when resource ownership is explicit.

Example resource decomposition:

```text
pointer.motion
pointer.buttons
keyboard
scroll
pen
contact.1
contact.2
```

A resident loop owning `pointer.motion` might coexist with a separately admitted keyboard one-shot. A planner command needing the same pointer resource should use one of:

1. queue until declared safe point;
2. pause resident program and transfer resource;
3. preempt/revoke when allowed;
4. reject/yield if no safe handoff exists.

Do not permit unsynchronized model pointer actions to race a resident pointer loop.

## Safe points and emergency revocation

Ordinary steering should usually apply only at explicit safe points:

```text
observe
-> evaluate
-> bounded action
-> verify/record
-> SAFE POINT
```

`REVOKE`, authority expiry, focus/surface loss and mandatory release must not wait for a cooperative safe point.

## Candidate high-value patterns

### 1. Watch-and-react during inference

```text
while model_thinking:
    watch target region
    if target appears:
        execute one preauthorized response
    if target becomes ambiguous:
        stop + interrupt planner
```

### 2. Maintain relation

```text
WHILE target_valid:
    keep target near center

ON target_centered:
    emit event / optional admitted one-shot
```

### 3. Repeat-until-effect

```text
repeat bounded action
observe fresh effect
stop when effect predicate is true
otherwise yield at budget/deadline
```

### 4. Prepared branch set

```text
IF state_A -> admitted future A
IF state_B -> admitted future B
ELSE -> YIELD
```

Runtime chooses only among semantic futures already authored by the model.

### 5. Inhibition / anti-action reflex

```text
WHILE action_controller_active:
    if target_identity_uncertain -> RELEASE
    if focus_changed             -> RELEASE
    if unexpected_modal          -> RELEASE
    if user_override             -> RELEASE
```

Resident programs should treat deterministic stop/inhibition paths as first-class, not only action triggers.

## Inference-time work classes

The architecture may benefit from explicitly distinguishing what local work is permissible while the model is unavailable:

```text
L0 OBSERVE_ONLY
    monitor / retain state/events

L1 NON_AUTHORITY_PREPARATION
    crops, target proposals, reversible/local computation

L2 BOUNDED_PREAUTHORIZED_EFFECT
    proven resident controller / admitted branch

L3 NEW_SEMANTIC_EFFECT
    wait for frontier-model decision / new authority
```

The runtime never upgrades itself from one class to another.

## H — first falsifiable hypothesis

For a controlled dynamic task whose relevant state can change during an intentionally delayed planner interval, a planner-installed resident recognition+execution program can preserve or improve independently scored useful response while reducing required planner boundaries, compared with:

1. planner polling/replanning only; and
2. a fixed open-loop macro;

without unauthorized actions, stale continuation, or release failures.

The first experiment does not need to claim general end-to-end speedup.

## T — first experimental ladder

### Rung 0 — semantics, no frontier model

Controlled fixture with one observable state transition and one bounded actuator.

Compare:

- `POLL_EXTERNAL`: external driver observes and submits each response;
- `OPEN_LOOP`: fixed periodic action regardless of state;
- `RESIDENT_REACTIVE`: one admitted state/edge recognizer triggers the action locally.

Inject a deterministic external delay to represent planner unavailability. Measure reaction, correctness and release. This isolates mechanism from model quality.

### Rung 1 — temporal edge, not level trigger

Show that `false -> true` fires exactly once while a persistent `true` state does not repeat indefinitely. Include transient-cue and absent-condition controls.

### Rung 2 — asynchronous steering

Start one resident loop; during execution deliver fresh-generation planner messages:

- valid parameter update;
- one-shot action on non-conflicting resource;
- same-resource pause/handoff;
- stale-generation delayed message;
- revoke.

Require deterministic disposition and final neutral resources.

### Rung 3 — real model interval

Only after mechanism gates pass, compare the same fixed model/task with and without the resident program during actual inference. Account for all model calls/tokens, local observations and effects.

## D — promotion rule

`PASS_RESIDENT_REACTIVE_PROGRAM_SCOPED` only if the resident arm:

- responds only to declared observable predicates/transitions;
- performs zero out-of-subset/out-of-authority actions;
- does not duplicate one-shot effects under persistent true state;
- stale-generation planner messages never affect current execution;
- same-resource interrupts follow the declared pause/preempt/reject protocol;
- cancel/expiry/focus loss neutralizes every owned resource;
- at least one useful state-triggered response occurs during the simulated or real planner-unavailable interval;
- independent application/effect scorer confirms the intended result.

`HOLD` if the fixture never creates an interval in which local reaction matters.

`REJECT` if resident execution becomes an unrestricted local planner, if asynchronous steering creates action races, or if equivalent behavior is already obtained more simply by #22 observation-only waiting.

## C — competing explanations / risks

- Benefit may come only from faster local sampling rather than the resident abstraction.
- Recognition can become a hidden application-specific semantic API.
- High-rate observation may cost more CPU/capture bandwidth than saved planner work.
- Persistent programs can continue a globally stale strategy even while locally correct.
- Too many interrupt semantics can become a second operating system.
- Reversible/preparatory actions may have hidden side effects.
- Multiple resident programs can deadlock/starve on shared resources unless arbitration is explicit.

Therefore begin with one resident program and one resource conflict before exploring multi-program scheduling.

## Relationship to the broader Agent Interface thesis

The intended division of labor is:

> The frontier model decides semantics and installs a temporary bounded reflex system. The Agent Interface keeps sensing, reacting and enforcing safety while the frontier model thinks, then lets the model steer or replace that reflex system when higher-level reasoning returns.

This treats frontier-model inference time as a period in which the environment remains live rather than as a mandatory system-wide pause.

It is one direct attempt to remove the I/O/control bottleneck without requiring a faster or less capable model.
